Initially, Udayaditya commands Sitaram to open the door and Sitaram obeys as a subordinate guard; later, during Udayaditya’s prison escape, Sitaram takes the lead, urges Udayaditya to flee, and physically carries him out, reversing their roles from commander‑subordinate to rescuer‑rescued.

Pratapaditya’s initial plan was to send two Pathan men to kill Basanta Ray when he stopped at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore, but the Pathans refused to carry out the killing. The method that finally succeeded was Pratapaditya’s order executed by Muktiyar Khan, who had Abdul strike Basanta Ray with a sword, killing him.
Inner quarters of the Jessore palace, disguised as a middle‑aged woman (Mother Nikasha); the king’s chamber/palace in Jessore, appearing as himself (the jester, undisguised).
Surma is secretly poisoned by Mangala (Rukmini).
Vibha discovers that the Maharaj is already marrying another woman and will not forgive her, shattering her hopes and leaving her heartbroken.

Rukmini took Udayaditya’s signet ring—bearing the Yubaraj’s seal—and Bhagavat used that ring to stamp a forged petition accusing the Yubaraj of treason, which Pratapaditya accepted as evidence to order Udayaditya’s imprisonment.

Ramchandra Ray’s midnight escape caused Pratapaditya to blame and dismiss the guards (Sitaram and Bhagavat); Udayaditya, feeling responsible for their dismissal, secretly arranged stipends for them with Surma’s aid, and when Pratapaditya learned of these secret stipends he ordered Surma to be sent to her paternal home.

The song conveys Basanta Ray’s sense of utter abandonment, emptiness, and longing for the loved ones who have vanished; he sings it first alone on his veranda in Raigarh at sunset, reflecting his personal solitude, and later in Jessore before the empty Surma room after Vibha tells him no one remains there, expressing the shared familial loss.

Rukmini’s inability to halt Udayaditya’s midnight escape allowed the prince to flee, which caused Pratapaditya to believe the Yubaraj had perished in the prison fire and to issue a death sentence for Basanta Ray—a sentence that Muktiyar Khan then carried out, killing Basanta Ray.

Pratapaditya received Ramchandra Ray with a cool, minimal welcome—barely acknowledging him and offering little honor—while later, in his own court, Ramchandra Ray openly disparages Pratapaditya’s status, mocking his lineage and treating him as clearly inferior.
She returns as the widow Mangala living on the outskirts of Jessore and prepares a poison that kills Surma, bringing tragedy to Udayaditya’s life.

Udayaditya formally renounces the throne by swearing an oath before the goddess Ma‑Kali that he will never accept any part of Jessore’s kingdom, will not sit on its throne, and will not even touch its royal scepter, thereby relinquishing his claim as crown prince.

It is intercepted by Nayanchand, given to the Mahishi, who then passes it to Basanta Ray; Basanta Ray instructs the Mahishi to tell Vibha that the letter requested she be sent to Chandradwip, thereby misrepresenting the letter’s actual spiteful content.
Pratapaditya had the canal beside the palace blocked with large sal‑wood logs, but Ramchandra’s party lifted the boat over those logs and continued downstream, thwarting the trap.

Basanta Ray’s once‑cherished sitar—his eternal companion—is abandoned or left unplayable: he tells Udayaditya he will leave the sitar behind and never play it again, later finds it missing or with broken strings that cannot be tuned, symbolizing his deepening despair over Udayaditya’s fate.

Earlier Udayaditya was ready to defend oppressed subjects—he would stop officials beating them and secretly provide financial aid—but after Surma’s death he grew fearful of Pratapaditya, hesitated in every matter, and refused to intervene, allowing oppression to continue unchecked.
He creates a fire at the prison, tells Udayaditya that the prison is on fire, and pulls him out, thereby freeing him from the unjust imprisonment caused by the forged petition.

He first ties the Maharaja to his back, descends a rope from the palace roof into the waiting boat and lowers him safely; later he lifts the unconscious Vibha and carries her out of the palace to a palanquin for escape.

In Jessore Vibha is lavishly adorned with eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and an elaborate hairstyle imposed by her mother‑in‑law, reflecting her status as a cherished daughter‑in‑law; in Chandradwip she appears as a plain, veiled common woman wearing simple clothing, no jewellery, her veil fallen, and she walks like a beggar or maidservant, having rejected all ornamentation.

In his bedchamber after Surma’s death, the window represents Udayaditya’s yearning for Surma’s return and the memory of her presence; in the prison cell, the small window becomes a symbol of hope for his own liberation, offering a glimpse of the sky and birds that reminds him freedom will one day come.

Initially, Sitaram flirtatiously borrows money from Rukmini, exchanging poetic promises and teasing banter while she pretends affection; but as his debts go unpaid, his visits become frequent and secretive, and his role in imprisoning the Yubaraj and setting the fire that kills Mangala is revealed, turning her love into vengeful rage—she curses him, arms herself with a blade, and attempts to kill him, transforming their playful financial liaison into a life‑threatening confrontation.

Sitaram’s fire began as a diversion to pull the guards away and allow Udayaditya to slip out, but he then turned it into a cover‑up by having his men sabotage firefighting, set the empty prison cell ablaze, plant bones, a skull and Udayaditya’s sword as false evidence, and spread the rumor that the Yubaraj had died in the blaze, thereby using the fire to conceal the escape.

Ramchandra Ray later interprets Udayaditya’s protective actions as being motivated solely by self‑interest—to safeguard his sister Vibha—and concludes that the rescue was obligatory rather than meritorious, so he feels no gratitude toward his brother‑in‑law.

By forging a petition in the name of Prince Udayaditya that accuses Pratapaditya of treason to the Emperor of Delhi, Pratapaditya uses the specter of the Emperor’s displeasure to label his son a traitor and have him imprisoned.

The grooming of Vibha’s hair—specifically Surma’s act of braiding it—marks Surma’s caring presence; when Surma is gone, Vibha’s hair remains unbraided as she waits in vain, signalling Surma’s tragic absence.
